lines.note: Umareki describes coming into this world through birth. The Portuguese Nacendo vir begins the definition, whose object continues on the next row; the printed principal forms remain unexpanded.
Mundo completes vir a este mundo, coming into this world. This short continuation belongs to Umareki and is not a separate entry.
Umaretsuki is being born with, or naturally possessing, a quality. The Portuguese introduces the innate-property sense developed in the example below.
The gloss ends with a natural quality, then Umaretsuita catagui- begins the statement that a disposition is inborn. The printed hyphen divides the Japanese example across physical rows.

runs.text: He cuſtume natural, ou com que naceo.

lines.note: Gia completes catagui gia: it is an inborn disposition. The Portuguese paraphrase specifies a custom or character with which one was born; cuſtume is preserved as printed.
Donni and riconni give the alternatives of being born dull or intelligent. The marker l introduces the second alternative; Na- begins the Portuguese translation on the next row.
Cer completes Nacer: to be born naturally foolish or discerning. Diſcreto supplies the positive counterpart of paruo and explains riconni above.
The noun Umaretsuki is glossed as nature or natural disposition. The final V- starts a repetition of the headword in the following example.
The example contrasts a person with a good or bad innate disposition. Maretçuqino joins the preceding V-, and Homem begins the Portuguese explanation.
De bom, ou ruim natural completes the description of a person of good or bad disposition. It continues the preceding Japanese example without adding a new sense.
Umarevochi denotes being born, with particular attention to the moment of birth. The following Portuguese rows delimit that moment rather than supplying a second headword.

runs.text: que declarão o tempo, em que hum nace logo

lines.note: The definition says this word expresses the time when someone is born, immediately on emerging. The phrase logo em continues into the next physical line.

runs.text: em ſaindo do ventre da mãy.

lines.note: Emerging from the mother's womb completes the definition of the birth moment. The scan shows a tilde in mãy; it is retained rather than regularized to modern mãe or the OCR's unmarked may.

runs.text: De pouco nacido, ou logo em

lines.note: Umarevochini means just after, or immediately upon, being born. De pouco nacido and logo em nacendo give the two closely related temporal paraphrases.
Nacendo completes logo em nacendo, immediately upon birth. The short row remains part of the Umarevochini entry.
Umarevotori means being born inferior or falling below one's ancestry. The Portuguese comparison starts with inferior a ou- and continues on the following row.

runs.text: tro, ou degenerar dos pays, ou antepaßados.

lines.note: Tro completes outro, followed by degenerating from one's parents or ancestors. The clause explains inherited inferiority, preserving the printed antepaßados spelling.
Umaumashii first describes something tasty and very savoury. The final sabro- continues as sabrosa on the following row; the figurative application is introduced afterwards.

runs.text: ſa. ¶ Item, permet. Quando hum faz

lines.note: Sa completes sabrosa, then the entry turns to a figurative use when someone does something well. The compressed permet. marker is left as printed.

runs.text: bem algũa couſa que contenta, ſe diz

lines.note: The figurative use concerns doing something pleasingly well. Vma v- begins the quoted expression umaumashii shiyoo, which crosses the line boundary.

runs.text: Modo de fazer as couſas bem

lines.note: Maxij completes the divided adjective, and xiyǒ denotes the manner of doing something. The Portuguese gloss begins a description of a well-executed way of acting.

runs.text: com artificio, ou a goſto dos outros. ¶

lines.note: Skill or artifice, and pleasing other people, complete the figurative explanation. The scan has a terminal V- starting the next example, not the OCR's isolated V followed by an italic full stop.
The example describes someone who says things agreeably or skilfully. Ma completes the preceding V-, and the Portuguese He ho- begins the corresponding description of the speaker.

runs.text: mem que diz as couſas com graça, & arti-

lines.note: Mem completes homem: a man who speaks with grace and artifice. The final arti- is physically divided and continues on the following row.
Ficio completes artificio and closes the description of the skilful speaker. The following derived forms belong to the same adjective but occupy their own row.

Umaumashisa and umaumashuu give the noun and adverbial forms of the preceding adjective. The scan supports long ſ in Vmavmaxiſa, correcting OCR f; this is a morphological reading aid, not grounds for modernizing the spelling.
Umavoi is a carrier or driver of pack animals, matched by Portuguese Almocreue. The printed vo sequence is preserved in the historical spelling.
Umaya is a stable, directly glossed by Eſtrebaria. This short, complete entry is independent of the following station-name compound.

runs.text: Lugares, ou eſtancias, onde ha ca-

lines.note: Umayagi names places or stations providing post horses. The visible initial in Lugares is L, not OCR D; ca- begins the word for horses on the next row.

runs.text: ualos dapoſta pera correos q̃ paſſão depreſa.

lines.note: The horses are for couriers travelling quickly. The phrase retains the printed dapoſta and abbreviation q̃ rather than expanding or respacing them.
Umayasaburai denotes a named area in noble households. The Portuguese locates that area relative to the horse stable in the following two rows.

runs.text: aßi chamado, que eſta logo junto, ou de fronte

lines.note: The named area stands immediately beside or opposite the stable. The spatial expression de fronte continues into the next row; aßi is the printed historical form.
The stable for the horses completes the location of the umayasaburai. It is the reference point of junto or de fronte above.
Umayoroi is horse armour or protective covering for a horse. The Portuguese distinguishes this equipment from an ordinary stable or saddle.
Pera pelejar gives the purpose of the horse covering: fighting. It completes the Umayoroi entry.

runs.text: Couas, ou poças que nos caminhos

lines.note: Umazacuri denotes hollows or puddle-like depressions left in roads. The definition continues with their formation by animals in mud.

runs.text: de lama deixão as beſtas quando paßão.

lines.note: These depressions are left by passing beasts on muddy roads. This completes the hoof-impression sense rather than describing deliberate excavation.

runs.text: O aiuntar, ou fazer gente de ca-

lines.note: Umazoroye is gathering or mustering mounted troops. The phrase gente de ca- continues with cauallo on the next row.
Vallo completes cauallo, and pouco vſado marks the expression as little used. The usage qualification belongs to the whole preceding entry.

runs.text: Molher eſteril, ou que não pare.

lines.note: Umazume is a woman who does not bear children, glossed as sterile. The printed historical wording and spelling are preserved without changing the definition.

Umazuqi means a person fond of horses. The scan supports Vmazuqi and inclinada, correcting the OCR intrusions in Vmnazuqi and inclixada; the opening is abraded but the remaining letter sequence and horse gloss agree. Independently read before comparison with NINJAL, whose headword index corroborates the identification (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).

runs.text: Iunta de caualos que andão no cã-

lines.note: Umazzure first denotes a group of horses roaming in the countryside. The nasal abbreviation in cã- is preserved across its physical division.

runs.text: po. ¶ Item permet. Companhia de gente

lines.note: Po completes the countryside reference, then a figurative use introduces a company of people. Their idle character is specified on the following row.
Vadia and ocioſa describe the company as wandering and idle. This completes the figurative extension of the horse-group expression.

runs.text: Certa fruita como ameixias, ou a-

lines.note: Ume names a fruit compared with plums, and then its tree. The scan reads ameixias, with a final s rather than OCR r; the tree name starts a- at the right edge.
Meixieira completes ameixieira, followed by Umenoqi for this tree. Both the fruit and tree senses remain within the printed explanation.

Ume is the verb for filling in or filling up, glossed Entulhar. The headword has no j: the OCR Vjme arose from the damaged initial area. Foriuo v- begins the example of filling a ditch, continued at the top of column 2.
Muru completes the divided verb from column 1: filling in a ditch. The next example begins Saqeni miz- for adding water to sake; its water noun continues below.
Zuuo completes mizzuuo, followed by vmuru, watering down sake. The Portuguese reads vinho, not OCR vinhe. Yu- introduces the next example involving hot water.
Ni attaches to the preceding Yu-: adding cold water to hot water. Botar agoa fria gives the physical action, while its purpose continues on the next row.
Temperar a quẽte specifies moderating the hot water with the cold addition. The tilde in quẽte remains an unexpanded abbreviation.
Umeague means filling something up to the top. The following Heike quotation illustrates filling an entire valley.
The Japanese quotation begins with one valley and the Heike force of seventy thousand. Xichiman carries the numerical meaning; the excess above that total is supplied by amari below.
Amariuo motte vmeague completes the description of filling with more than the stated number. Feiq. is a citation label, and italic Lib. introduces the book number on the next row.
Book 3 is cited, followed by a Portuguese rendering of filling right to the top. The translation's object, one valley, continues into the next line.

runs.text: valle com mais de ſetenta milhomens mortos da

lines.note: The valley is filled with more than seventy thousand dead men. The tight printed milhomens is retained rather than separated according to modern word spacing.

Parte do Feique identifies the dead as belonging to the Heike side. This closes the quoted illustration of filling the valley. Feique remains italic as printed, while it is recorded as an embedded Japanese name for optional typeface review.
Umeauaxe means mixing or tempering one thing with another. The scan has e in Vmeauaxe, not the OCR's Vmcauaxe; its printed principal forms remain unchanged.

runs.text: rar hũa couſa com outra como vinho com a-

lines.note: The definition describes tempering one substance with another, exemplified by wine and water. The final a- starts agoa across the physical line break.
Goa completes agoa and closes the mixing example. The small continuation belongs wholly to Umeauaxe.
Umeboxi denotes salted plums, with the drying process described below. The printed Portuguese capital in Ameixias is preserved.
Cas completes secas: the plums are dried in the sun. This process explains the compound umeboshi without changing the historical headword spelling.

runs.text: Entulho, ou couſa cõ q̃ entulhão as

lines.note: Umecusa names fill or material used to fill excavations. The Portuguese abbreviations cõ and q̃ remain unexpanded; the object as cauas continues below.

runs.text: cauas. ¶ Item, permet. Soldados, ou gente

lines.note: Cauas completes the literal filling material definition, then a figurative sense introduces soldiers or people. The military application is explained in the next two rows.

runs.text: que ſe manda diante como entulho, porque logo

lines.note: These people are sent ahead as expendable filling, because they are expected to fall immediately. The imagery connects the military use directly to the literal entulho.

runs.text: ande ſer mortos, ou ficar no campo.

lines.note: The soldiers are to be killed or left on the field. The printed ande is retained, without supplying letters or modernizing it to a contemporary Portuguese construction.
Umenoqi cross-refers to Ume, the fruit-tree entry near the end of column 1. The referenced Japanese word Vme is printed within the italic cross-reference apparatus.
Umeqi denotes groaning, directly glossed by Gemer. The printed qu and eita are abbreviated principal forms and remain unexpanded; the derived kana hint is not diplomatic text.

runs.text: O tingir com pao que he como de

lines.note: Umezome is dyeing with wood likened to plum wood. The preparation of that material is specified in the following row.
The wood is cooked or boiled in water to make the dye. The printed nagoa contraction and the paired cozido or feruido are retained.

runs.text: Salmoura de certa fruita como amei-

lines.note: Umezu is brine from a sour fruit compared to plums. The fruit comparison continues across amei- and xias on the next physical row.
Xias azedas completes the sour-plum comparison. Umezuuo ſaſu introduces adding this brine, with the Portuguese Miſtu- continuing below.

runs.text: rar eſta ſalmoura, ou vinagre pera tingir de

lines.note: The brine or vinegar is mixed in for dyeing. The scan supports ſalmoura, matching the clearly printed Salmoura above and correcting OCR ſabmoura.
Vermelho fino gives the intended rich red colour. It completes the dyeing application of umezu.
Umezzuqe denotes salted or preserved plums. The nasal abbreviation in cõſerua is preserved rather than expanded.
This Umi entry means giving birth; Couo vmu illustrates bearing a child. The abbreviated principal forms are retained exactly, without supplying an expected consonant before u.
Parir filho, ou filha explains the example as bearing a son or daughter. It belongs to the childbirth verb, not to the following homograph.
The next Umi means ripening, applied to fruit or to an abscess coming to a head. The tight afruita and oua- remain as printed across the line break.
Poſtema completes apoſtema, the abscess example in the ripening definition. The word is not silently replaced by a modern medical term.
This Umi is illustrated by Vouo vmu, working or joining hemp fibres into thread. Ajun- begins the Portuguese description of bringing the fibres together.

runs.text: tar, & pegar o linho canemo hum no outro tor

lines.note: Tar completes Ajuntar, followed by joining hemp fibres to one another. Tor continues as torcendo on the next row; no hyphen is supplied where the printed edge does not establish one.

runs.text: cendoo pera depois ſe fazerem linhas, ou

lines.note: The fibres are twisted so that thread or yarn can subsequently be made. The scan reads pera, correcting OCR peta; the purpose clause continues below.
Fiado completes the yarn-making explanation. This short continuation closes the hemp-working verb entry.
The next Umi means becoming tired or weary. Ga- begins a maxim about study, distinct from the preceding verbs with the same romanized headword.
Gacumonni vmucoto nacare means do not grow weary of learning. The negative imperative nacare is matched by the Portuguese Não vos enfadeis across this and the next row.
Fadeis completes the Portuguese prohibition: do not become weary of study. This closes the example attached to the fatigue verb.
Umi here is the noun for the sea, directly glossed Mar. It is separate from both the preceding verb and the following noun for pus.
This homonymous Umi means pus or discharge. Materia and vurmo are the Portuguese explanatory terms; the latter is retained in its historical spelling.

runs.text: Hũa cinta de pao que fica mais ale-

lines.note: Umiari describes a raised wooden band on a saddle. The word divided at the edge is ale- followed by uantada, correcting OCR alt-; the definition concerns saddle construction.
The wooden band stands higher on the saddle arch. Umiarino begins the example of a saddle fitted with this band, continued with cura below.

runs.text: Sella que tem eſta cinta, ou taboa.

lines.note: Cura completes Umiarino cura, a saddle with this wooden band or board. The Portuguese retains the explanatory pairing cinta or taboa.
Uminaxino cura gives the contrasting saddle without that band. The Portuguese Aque a não tem is retained with its printed tight spacing.
Umibata denotes the shore or edge of the sea. The short Portuguese Borda do mar provides a complete independent definition.

runs.text: Certo mariſco do mar comprido como

lines.note: Umidaqe is a long marine shellfish compared with little tubes. The scan has como at the right edge, correcting OCR com; its comparison continues on the next row.
The small white tubes complete the shellfish comparison. The far-right Vmi- on this baseline is a separate catchword anticipating the following page, not part of the Portuguese definition.

The far-right catchword anticipates Vmigoxi at the beginning of f539. Its short terminal mark is heavily inked and rounded; Vmi- is retained as the chosen reading. It shares the last body row's baseline but is separate page furniture.
